transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-16 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (LatticeCast CTO), Luis Ortega (LatticeCast ML Eng), Hannah Park (Infra Lead), Samir Rao (Product), Olivia Kim (Data Eng)
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/ff-20260716-lattice-8432 (note: link for reference)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be fuzzy):
- Short: caching shows strong token-dollar wins for short repetitive prefixes; batching improves tokens/sec but increases p95; need targeted bench with LatticeCast prompts.

--- Transcript body (timestamps approx every 30-60s, auto transcription errors possible) ---
[00:00] Jordan: alright everyone, hello, thanks for joining the weekly LatticeCast sync. um i'm Jordan, i'll run the agenda quick. priya's gonna share the benchmark notes, then we'll go through a few anomalies on the 8k context runs.
[00:15] Priya: hey hi. um quick note, i pushed the bench results into the shared sheet, link in chat — one caveat, the quant numbers here were run on our internal dev pool not the dedicated slot so latency variance is a bit higher.
[00:28] Olivia: got it, seeing the sheet now. there's a tab called "kv-snap" with cache/no-cache.
[00:35] Priya: yeah that one. quick callout — with prefix cache enabled, tokens/sec improves roughly 2.8x for the 512-1k prompt range, but for >6k we saw throughput dip and p95 jump unexpectedly.
[00:51] Luis: is that because of KV cache miss on long sequences or memory churn with kv?
[00:56] Priya: exactly the hypothesis. when the sequence grows, the KV footprint grows, which pushes some kernel choices and memory movement. we think the runtime is switching to a different attention kernel at about 6.5k that isn't as batch-friendly.
[01:12] Maya: hmm, for our use case most requests are ~700-1200 tokens with a 6k retrieval context appended for background. so mix is mid-long not pure long.
[01:25] Jordan: thanks for clarifying. so the important metric for you is tokens per dollar for the mixed distribution and p95 latency for the interactive flows — correct?
[01:34] Maya: yes, and secondarily the ability to hit 99th percentile SLOs during peak times.
[01:39] Priya: ok, so two axes: optimize tokens/$ for bulk summarization and keep p95 under 450ms for interactive. we recommend caching for repeated retrieval segments and small-ish batch sizes for interactive to reduce p95.
[01:55] Hannah: what's small-ish? 4? 8?
[01:58] Priya: start at 4-8 for 1-2k sequences. for shorter prompts batching of 16 was fine, but that pushes p95 above your target in our tests.
[02:11] Samir: curious about autoscale config — if we reserve a dedicated pool, does Redwood autoscale within it? we want to avoid paying for idle GPUs but keep warm capacity for spikes.
[02:20] Jordan: yes. dedicated pools can be configured with min/max and burst. you can set min to handle normal and burst to handle spikes; pricing is different for reserved vs burst usage. i'll share a recommended config in the spreadsheet.
[02:34] Luis: we also noticed tokens/sec/$ dropped significantly when we enabled 8-bit quantization in one run, is that expected?
[02:40] Priya: there can be a hit depending on operator support and kernel selection. quant helps memory and can allow bigger batch sizes, but some model ops are slower in our quant path depending on the model. which model variant are you on?
[02:51] Olivia: using lc-small-8k-v2 (our dev fork).
[02:55] Priya: ok that helps, we've seen that variant picks a fallback kernel for some attention types. part of the follow-up is to run the variants across our kernel matrix.
[03:08] Hannah: can you summarize the worst-case tokens/sec per dollar we've seen so we can plan budget?
[03:14] Priya: worst-case with long 8k+ and no cache, small batch, quant off, we measured ~450 tokens per dollar per second — it's the low end. With prefix cache and medium batch, we hit up to ~2,400 tokens/sec/$ on the 512-1k portion. averaged over your mix it looked like ~1,100 tokens/sec/$.
[03:36] Maya: that's a big spread. how do we get the average closer to the 2k region without blowing p95?
[03:43] Priya: two levers 1) aggressive prefix/KV caching — since your retrieval content repeats across users — that reduces per-request decode tokens. 2) stratified routing: route short interactive to low-latency pool with small batch, route bulk summarization to a higher-throughput pool with aggressive batching and quant.
[04:01] Luis: does routing add complexity on our side? we have to tag requests?
[04:06] Jordan: you can either call different endpoints or include a header that our routing layer recognizes. we can provide SDK hooks to make it transparent.
[04:14] Samir: earlier we ran a trace capture for an outlier where p95 spiked to 1.2s; i uploaded traces in the sheet under traces/2026-07-12.zip
[04:23] Priya: i pulled that. looking at the trace there was a cache miss followed by a long disk io wait on the infra side — hannah can comment — but also the runtime did a kernel switch right before decode which adds ~220ms.
[04:37] Hannah: the disk io note — that was from our retrieval microservice hitting its cold-start on S3; we were seeing higher tail from the retrieval. we'll enable a keep-warm policy.
[04:46] Olivia: question — what's the interplay between prefix caching and kv-cache? are they the same?
[04:51] Priya: good question. by prefix cache here i mean storing tokenized KV entries so the model can re-use KV state; it's orthogonal to external retrieval caching. we observed the internal KV cache reduces decode tokens because many token prefixes skip recomputation. the retrieval cache reduces what you pass to the model in the first place. combine both and you get multiplicative wins.
[05:12] Luis: great. on the bench you mentioned a weird dip at 6k where tokens/sec fell off. is that a hard threshold we can tune?
[05:19] Priya: it's model+runtime interplay. there's a kernel selection boundary when total KV size exceeds a threshold tied to GPU memory layout. sometimes we can change the kernel heuristics; in other cases quantization or changing the padding/truncation strategy helps. i'll run a targeted test to see if small changes in chunking push the threshold out.
[05:36] Jordan: quick pricing note — current pilot pricing in the sheet assumes X throughput baseline; if we can demonstrate sustained 1.8k tokens/sec/$ on your mix we can adjust the pilot credits. i'll annotate the sheet with scenarios.
[05:50] Maya: that would help sell internally. our finance folks want conservative numbers.
[05:55] Priya: action: i'll do a 24h KV-cache focused run using your exact prompt set (Priya -> LatticeCast prompts) and include p50/p95/p99 tokens/sec/$ and memory profile.
[06:06] Maya: ok, please include the tail percentiles.
[06:09] Priya: will do.
[06:11] [00:06:11] Jordan: a quick thread on security — Hannah, you flagged wanting audit logs and SSO before canary. where are we?
[06:19] Hannah: we already have SAML SSO integrated in dev, but audit retention and KMS integration needs to be verified in the private plane. for pilot we need audit-forwarding to our Splunk.
[06:29] Jordan: note — Redwood supports audit log export and KMS/HSM integration in Private. for hosted pilot we can enable audit streaming (with some PII redaction options). i'll put the security doc in the follow-up packet.
[06:42] Samir: do we need an on-prem agent to forward logs, or is it push to Splunk?
[06:48] Jordan: either — we can push directly to your splunk ingest endpoint or you can run a small forwarder in your VPC. Hannah, we'll send options.
[06:55] Priya: back to bench — a small note about batching: for short prompts batching of 16 increases tokens/sec by ~35% with p95 bump of ~150ms. for your interactive SLO that isn't acceptable. but for the summarization worker, batching of 64 with quant gave the best tokens/$ with acceptable latency.
[07:20] Olivia: curious about scaling: if we run the high-throughput pool, does it require a different model artifact?
[07:25] Priya: usually same model artifact with different runtime flags (quant vs fp16) and different kernel scheduling; sometimes we create a slim variant optimized for throughput. that requires a quick onboarding step but we can do it in the pilot.
[07:39] Luis: are there any security/compliance blockers for us? we're in fintech so SOC2/ISO-ish matters.
[07:45] Jordan: Redwood has SOC 2 Type II and ISO docs; for Private deployments we support on-prem and VPC plus KMS. i'll attach the compliance packet.
[07:55] Maya: perfect.
[07:59] [00:07:59] Priya: ok, next recurring piece — canary plan. propose: reserve a small dedicated pool with min=2 GPUs for interactive (p95 target) and a separate burstable pool for batch summarization. run a 48h canary, trace and compare tokens/sec/$ and adjust. thoughts?
[08:20] Hannah: that seems reasonable. can we time it for low-traffic window?
[08:24] Jordan: yes, week of 7/27 we suggested. i'll put a calendar invite once dates confirmed.
[08:31] Samir: one more question — competitor benchmarking. have you run side-by-side against bedrock or anthopic?
[08:39] Priya: we've done internal comparisons; public cloud endpoints vary a lot on kernel choices. it's in our research notes but not apples-to-apples unless we match model variants. if you want we'll run a focused comparo on your representative prompt set.
[08:54] Maya: i'd like that, especially latency tail comparisons.
[08:57] Jordan: action on us to scope that and include estimate in the sheet.
[09:02] Olivia: any quick wins we can flip this week?
[09:05] Priya: enable retrieval keep-warm to avoid S3 cold-starts, reduce interactive batch to 4, enable prefix cache on the runtime side for repeated retrieval segments. those three should move the needle this week.
[09:19] Hannah: implement keep-warm today and share results.
[09:22] Jordan: great.
[09:24] Maya: ok if we summarize the decisions: 1) run 24h KV bench (Priya), 2) enable keep-warm (LatticeCast), 3) Jordan to update pricing and schedule canary. anything else?
[09:36] Priya: also we'll test small chunking tweaks to push the kernel boundary out for >6k contexts.
[09:42] Jordan: thanks all, i'll follow up with the packet: bench plan, pricing sheet, security docs, canary schedule.
[09:50] Maya: thanks everyone.
[09:53] [00:09:53] Recording bot: meeting ended.

End of transcript. Some names/terms may be mis-transcribed (e.g., kernel heuristics, kv vs k v cache).
